title: Oona and the Bobbing Shells
markdown:
Oona lived in a grotto shaped like a sea-anemone bloom, tucked among swaying kelp and quiet coral. Outside, the sand was a highway for darting fish, but Oona loved the treasures that tumbled down from the world above. Smooth shells that whispered of farther water. Pebbles worn round by tides. Bits of sea-glass that caught the sun when it reached the reef.

She wanted her grotto to be the most beautiful home in the reef, a careful display of those wonders.

One bright morning she found a pile of splendid shells: swirly spirals, speckled ones like tiny night skies, and one shaped like a rolled-up scroll. Her eight arms wiggled. This was her chance.

She tried to scoop them all at once. Four plump shells in one arm, three more in another, the last in a third, her other arms helping to balance. When she swam away, her arms grew heavy, much heavier than usual. The smooth shells slipped. Splash. Treasures tumbled back to the sandy bottom, scattering like fallen jewels. Oona sighed, a stream of bubbly disappointment. She tried again, fewer this time, only three. Still, as she kicked forward, the shells danced out of her grasp one by one. The colours seemed to dim as her hope dwindled. She sat on the sand and counted her arms, as if eight might suddenly become enough if she asked politely.

Down on the seabed, Ferris the crab was sorting shiny seaweed. He had watched. He noticed how the lighter, more open shells bobbed for a moment on the current before they sank, while the heavier, compact ones went straight down like little stones.

He scuttled closer, legs tapping softly on the sand.

“Oona,” he called, a gentle rasp like pebbles in surf. “You are trying to carry too much at once.”

Oona nodded, tentacles drooping.

“Look closely.” Ferris nudged a hollow, wide-mouthed shell. It bobbed on the incoming current, as if happy to be carried. Then he pushed a smaller, denser one. It sank at once.

“Some things like to float,” Ferris said. “Some like to sink. It depends on what they are.” He pointed at the bobbing shell. “This wide one has lots of space inside. It holds air, and that makes it lighter in the water, like a little boat. The water lifts it. The solid ones have less air, so they are heavier for their size, and they go down.”

The kelp swayed. Sunlight moved in slow coins on the sand. Oona watched, eyes wide. The water was not only something to swim in. It had its own ways.

Ferris showed her how to pick the lighter, wider shells, the ones that seemed to dance. He stacked them one above another, like careful building blocks, and showed her how to use her suckers to hold them gently, spreading the weight along her arms.

Oona followed. She gathered several and swam slowly, gently. The shells bobbed and danced around her, but they stayed. She managed five back to her grotto, and then another five, and then five more. The grotto began to fill with shimmering treasures. Her heart felt as wide as the water.

She sat a while, content, watching the light play on the new shells. Water moved through the grotto mouth in a long, easy breath. A small fish looked in and went away, unbothered. Kelp leaned, leaned back. Oona did not rush. That was when it clicked: the wide shells wanted to be boats. The solid ones wanted to be stones. She had been treating them all the same.

“Ferris,” she said at last, arms full of another chosen batch, “how did you know?”

Ferris did a little scuttle-dance. “It is called buoyancy. That is a word for how well something floats. It depends on shape and what is inside. A big empty ship can sail, even though it is huge. A small solid rock sinks. The water pushes up. Some things let it. Some do not.”

Oona looked at her decorated grotto, then at Ferris. “Buoyancy,” she whispered, trying the word. “A secret game the water plays.” She giggled, a sound like tiny bells underwater. “I wonder if the water can help me find other treasures. Or even build new things.”

Ferris smiled, pleased. The current lifted the wide shells a fraction, as if agreeing to keep playing, and Oona’s grotto held its quiet shine while she watched, already wondering what else the water might lift.
